bible_refs.method: wording: Latin heading = Vulgate 'omnis qui occiderit Cain septuplum punietur'; Greek lemma = LXX 'πᾶς ὁ ἀποκτείνας Καιν ἑπτὰ ἐκδικούμενα παραλύσει'
bible_refs.note: Two forms of the verse: the editor's Latin heading follows the Vulgate, the letter quotes the LXX; rendered differently on purpose.
Paul's charge to Timothy, cited by name in the letter.

choices.why: The letter explains the verse as the killer ending Cain's sevenfold penalty; παραλύω is to release or undo.
rejected: will be punished sevenfold (the Vulgate sense, kept only in the Latin heading)

choices.why: Answered by Ἔπειτα καί at the start of the next section.
Idiom for something talked of on every side; the literal phrase is a calque.
Covers both kinship and household closeness; the Greek does not say which.

pass_a_gloss: [Latin editorial heading] Letter LXXX. To Optimus the bishop. On those words: 'Everyone who will have killed Cain will be punished sevenfold.' [Greek] And otherwise gladly seeing the good boys, both because of the steadiness of their manners beyond their age, and because of their closeness/kinship toward your reverence, from which it is possible to expect something great too in them. Since with your letters I saw them approaching me, I doubled my affection for them. When I read the letter and saw in it at once the providential care of your disposition concerning the churches, and at once the diligence concerning the reading of the divine Scriptures, I gave thanks to the Lord, and prayed for good things for those who conveyed such letters to us, and before them for the one who wrote to us. You sought out that much-talked-of saying, carried around up and down among all: what solution has 'Whoever kills Cain will release seven things avenged/punishments'? Through this, first of all, you commended yourself, as accurately keeping the [precept] of Timothy, as Paul gave it to him; for you are clearly attending to the reading.
pass_b_english: Letter 80. To Bishop Optimus. On the words, “Whoever kills Cain will be punished sevenfold” (Genesis 4:15).

In any case I am glad to see these good boys, both for the steadiness of character that is beyond their years and for their close tie to Your Reverence, from which one may expect something great of them. When I saw them coming to me with a letter of yours, I doubled my affection for them. And when I read the letter and saw in it both your provident care for the churches and your diligence in reading the divine Scriptures, I gave thanks to the Lord, and I prayed for blessings on those who brought us such a letter, and before them on the one who wrote it to us.

You asked about that much-discussed saying, repeated everywhere by everyone: what is the solution to “Whoever kills Cain will release seven punishments” (Genesis 4:15)? In this, first of all, you have commended yourself as one who carefully keeps the charge to Timothy, just as Paul gave it to him; for you are plainly attending to reading (1 Timothy 4:13).
source_text:
Ad Optimum episcopum
EPISTOLA LXXX. AD OPTIMUM EPISCOPUM. In illa verba: "Omnis qui
occiderit Cain, septuplum punietur."
77.365
Καὶ ἄλλως ἡδέως ὁρῶν τοὺς ἀγαθοὺς παῖδας, διά τε τὸ ὑπὲρ τὴν ἡλικίαν τῶν
ἠθῶν εὐσταθὲς, καὶ διὰ τὸ πρὸς τὴν σὴν εὐλάβειαν οἰκεῖον, ἀφ' οὗ τι καὶ μέγα
προσδοκᾷν ἔστιν ἐπ' αὐτοῖς. Ἐπειδὴ μετὰ γραμμάτων σῶν εἶδον αὐτοὺς προσιόντας
μοι, ἐδιπλασίασα τὸ ἐπ' αὐτοῖς φίλτρον. Ὅτε δὲ ἀνέγνων τὴν ἐπιστολὴν, καὶ ἴδον ἐν
αὐτῇ ὁμοῦ μὲν τὸ περὶ τὰς Ἐκκλησίας προνοητικὸν τῆς διαθέσεως, ὁμοῦ δὲ περὶ τὴν
ἀνάγνωσιν τῶν θείων Γραφῶν ἐπιμελὲς, ηὐχαρίστησα τῷ Κυρίῳ, καὶ ἐπηυξάμην τὰ
ἀγαθὰ τοῖς τὰ τοιαῦτα ἡμῖν διακομίσασι γράμματα, καὶ πρό γε αὐτῶν τῷ γράψαντι
ἡμῖν. Ἐπεζήτησας τὸ πολυθρύλλητον ἐκεῖνο, καὶ παρὰ πᾶσιν ἄνω καὶ κάτω
περιφερόμενον ῥητὸν, τίνα τὴν λύσιν ἔχει τὸ, Ὁ πᾶς ἀποκτείνας Καΐν, ἑπτὰ
ἐκδικούμενα παραλύσει; ∆ιὰ δὲ τούτου τέως 77.368 μὲν αὐτὸς ἑαυτὸν συνέστησας, τὸ
Τιμοθέου, ὥσπερ ἔδωκεν Παῦλος αὐτῷ, ἀκριβῶς φυλάσσοντα· δῆλος γὰρ εἶ
προσέχων τῇ ἀναγνώσει.
reviewer: claude (Wave A review, clause by clause against the Greek)
review_notes: Author: this letter is Basil of Caesarea's Letter 260, to Bishop Optimus. PG 77 prints it among the letters of Cyril of Alexandria as Letter 80. Identity checked against the Greek and against the NPNF Series 2 vol. 8 English of Basil's Letter 260 (used only to confirm identity, not for wording).

Reviewer rv0 fixes applied before merge: τέως μέν as 'first of all'; no 'But' before Ἐπειδή (no particle in the Greek); καὶ ἄλλως as 'in any case'; ἄνω καὶ κάτω περιφερόμενον as 'repeated everywhere by everyone'.
Checked clean: the Latin heading (Vulgate Genesis 4:15), the Septuagint lemma, 1 Timothy 4:13.
The book metadata title 'Letter to Optatus' did not match the addressee (Optimus); corrected to 'Letter to Bishop Optimus'.
